extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing definitions, proof techniques, and examples for injective, surjective, and bijective functions; composition and inverse functions; and the axiom of choice. Focus is on how to prove properties and construct or refute inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective (one-to-one)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : A → B is injective when if a1 ≠ a2 then f(a1) ≠ f(a2); equivalently, if f(a1) = f(a2) then a1 = a2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the term 'injective' over 'one-to-one' to avoid prepositional slip-ups. A common student mistake is to assert the converse (a1 = a2 ⇒ f(a1) = f(a2)), which merely states the function is well defined. Proof techniques: proving f(a1)=f(a2) ⇒ a1=a2 (use algebra/manipulation or contrapositive). Consequence: for finite sets, an injection A→B implies |A| ≤ |B|. Preimage behavior: the preimage of a singleton under an injection is either empty or contains exactly one element. Examples: f(x)=7x−3 is injective; f(x)=x^2 on R is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjective (onto)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : A → B is surjective when for every b ∈ B there exists some a ∈ A with f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: every element of the codomain is hit by the function. Proof technique: given an arbitrary y ∈ B, explicitly choose x (often by solving y = f(x)) and show x lies in the domain and f(x)=y. You do not have to explain how you discovered the choice of x in the formal proof, though adding intuition can help readers. To show non-surjectivity find a b ∈ B with no preimage (e.g., x^2 : R → R is not surjective because −1 has no preimage). Consequence: for finite sets, a surjection A→B implies |A| ≥ |B|. Preimage behavior: for surjections, the preimage of any singleton is non-empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective (one-to-one correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : A → B is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bijection provides a one-to-one correspondence and is a certificate that two (finite) sets have the same cardinality (|A| = |B|). Bijective functions have unique inverses. Construction or verification can be done by proving injectivity and surjectivity separately, or by explicitly giving an inverse and checking it composes to the identity. Examples: identity function i_A is bijective; certain restricted x^2 maps (e.g., [0,∞)→[0,∞)) are bijections; Möbius transformations (with ad ≠ bc and appropriate domain/codomain adjustments) can be bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preimage behaviour for singletons
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B and b ∈ B, the preimage f^{-1}({b}) has constrained sizes depending on injectivity/surjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f is injective then f^{-1}({b}) is either empty or contains exactly one element. If f is surjective then f^{-1}({b}) is non-empty (contains at least one element). Use these facts when constructing inverses or arguing existence/uniqueness of preimage elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving injectivity (recommended proof patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard approach: assume f(a1) = f(a2) and deduce a1 = a2; alternatively use the contrapositive form: a1 ≠ a2 ⇒ f(a1) ≠ f(a2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic manipulation of equalities is often easiest (students have more practice with equalities). Example proof provided for f(x)=7x−3: set f(a1)=f(a2), simplify to get a1=a2. Emphasize avoiding the incorrect converse implication. Include counterexamples when necessary to show failure of injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving surjectivity (recommended proof patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard approach: let y ∈ B be arbitrary, construct or choose x ∈ A such that f(x) = y, and verify f(x)=y and x ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often done by algebraically solving y = f(x) for x and then checking the candidate lies in the domain. Authors note: it's acceptable in a formal proof to state 'Given y choose x = ...' and verify; you need not show how you discovered the formula for x, though explaining the derivation in surrounding text can aid intuition. Example: for f(x)=7x−3 solve x=(y+3)/7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuting injectivity/surjectivity by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-injective: exhibit a1 ≠ a2 with f(a1) = f(a2). Non-surjective: exhibit b ∈ B such that for every a ∈ A, f(a) ≠ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are existential negations of the universal properties. Example: f(x)=x^2 on R is non-injective because f(−1)=f(1)=1; it is non-surjective because −1 ∈ R is not in the image. Make the existence explicit and check conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition: preservation of properties, associativity, and non-commutativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f : A→B and g : B→C, (g◦f) : A→C is defined by (g◦f)(a)=g(f(a)). Composition is associative but generally not commutative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f and g are both injective then g◦f is injective. If f and g are both surjective then g◦f is surjective. Consequently, composition of bijections is a bijection. Proofs: combine definitions; associativity follows from the evaluation rule g(f(a)). Use diagrams or element-wise arguments to justify. Examples and counterexamples illustrate failure of commutativity and show how properties may fail to transfer backward from composition to components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deducing component properties from composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If g◦f is injective then f must be injective. If g◦f is surjective then g must be surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: injective case — assume f(a1)=f(a2), apply g to get equal images, then use injectivity of g◦f to conclude a1=a2. Surjective case — for given c ∈ C, use surjectivity of g◦f to find a ∈ A with g(f(a))=c, take b=f(a) to demonstrate g(b)=c. Examples show the converses need not hold (g may fail injectivity even if g◦f is injective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Left-inverse and right-inverse definitions and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A→B and g : B→A: g is a left-inverse of f if g◦f = i_A; g is a right-inverse of f if f◦g = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f has a left-inverse then f is injective; if f has a right-inverse then f is surjective. Examples with small finite sets illustrate functions that have only a left- or only a right-inverse. Note: having both left- and right-inverse implies bijectivity and the two one-sided inverses coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of true inverse functions
rubrics_metrics.description: f has a two-sided inverse (g with g◦f = i_A and f◦g = i_B) if and only if f is bijective. Any such inverse is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior lemmas: left-inverse ⇔ injective; right-inverse ⇔ surjective; if both hold the one-sided inverses are equal. Proof of uniqueness uses simple composition identities. To exhibit an inverse either prove bijectivity or explicitly construct g and verify the two composition equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing one-sided inverses and the Axiom of Choice remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct left-inverse for injective f by assigning to each b ∈ B the unique preimage a if exists, otherwise an arbitrary α ∈ A. Construct right-inverse for surjective f by choosing any element from each non-empty preimage Ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite collections of preimages this construction is straightforward; for infinite families the step 'choose an element from each preimage' can require the Axiom of Choice. The text flags that selecting an element from infinitely many non-empty sets in general needs AC, but when preimages are singletons (e.g., f injective) AC is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality implications and beware converses
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists an injection f : A→B between finite sets then |A| ≤ |B|. If there exists a surjection g : A→B then |A| ≥ |B|. However, the converse statements (|A| ≤ |B| ⇒ all f : A→B are injections, etc.) are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning 10.4.9 emphasises not to confuse existence of an injection/surjection with properties of arbitrary functions between sets of given sizes. Use explicit counterexamples (diagrams/functions) to exhibit failures of the converses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-writing and style notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice about language and presentation in proofs concerning functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise terminology (injective/surjective/bijective) to colloquial 'one-to-one/onto' to avoid prepositional errors. Be careful about direction of logical implications (avoid giving the converse). When demonstrating existence (e.g., surjectivity) it's acceptable to state the correct choice and verify it rather than show the discovery process; adding intuitive explanation can help readers but isn't required for correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling domain/codomain restrictions in formulas (Möbius examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the explicit formula for a function has singularities or values that cannot be attained, remove the offending points from the domain/codomain and treat the function accordingly (e.g., Möbius transforms require removing x = d/c from domain and a/c from codomain when ad ≠ bc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate injectivity and surjectivity by algebraic manipulation while respecting the adjusted domain/codomain. For Möbius transforms show injectivity by cross-multiplying denominators (taking care denominators ≠ 0) and surjectivity by solving for x in terms of y and checking the solution lies in the (restricted) domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice: definition, finite-case construction, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A choice function on a collection 𝒮 of non-empty sets assigns to each X ∈ 𝒮 an element f(X) ∈ X. For finite collections a choice function exists (proof by induction); the Axiom of Choice asserts existence for arbitrary collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalences and consequences: AC ⇔ the Cartesian product of any collection of non-empty sets is non-empty; AC implies the Well-ordering theorem and results like Banach–Tarski. The text gives intuitive finite examples (choose smallest element in subsets of N, left shoe vs socks) and flags that some striking consequences are non-intuitive. For rigorous selection from infinitely many non-empty sets one generally needs AC; references and further reading suggested.
